title: Mueller report documents Stone’s WikiLeaks claims and campaign contacts
description_short: Mueller described Stone’s WikiLeaks claims and campaign contacts; it did not establish Trump’s advance knowledge of Podesta’s October 7 release.
description_medium: The Mueller report recounts Roger Stone’s statements about expected WikiLeaks releases and his contacts with Trump campaign associates. It also describes campaign officials’ efforts to learn about potential disclosures. The report does not establish that Trump received advance notice of the specific October 7, 2016 publication of John Podesta’s emails, or that Stone’s texts prove such knowledge.
description_long: Volume I of Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s report recounts Roger Stone’s claims that WikiLeaks would release damaging material and describes contacts between Stone and Trump campaign figures about possible releases. The report discusses Paul Manafort’s and Rick Gates’s accounts concerning what campaign officials heard about Stone’s claimed access and anticipated disclosures. These accounts support that some campaign figures treated Stone as a potential source of updates. They do not establish that Trump knew in advance of WikiLeaks’ October 7, 2016 publication of John Podesta’s emails; discussion of possible releases is not proof that Trump received notice of that specific publication. The record should distinguish witness recollections and contacts described by investigators from the stronger conclusion in the original title. The official report is the primary source for what the investigation said, and the corrected entry stays within its account of Stone and campaign communications rather than claiming that the report found advance presidential knowledge.
notes: Source-correction proposal only; no canonical or database record was changed.

title: FDA suspends food-laboratory quality checks after staffing cuts
description_short: Reuters reported that FDA suspended a food-laboratory proficiency-testing program after staffing cuts at its Moffett Center.
description_medium: Reuters reported on April 17, 2025, that FDA suspended a proficiency-testing program used to check consistency across its Food Emergency Response Network of about 170 food-testing labs. The agency attributed the suspension to HHS staffing cuts that removed several key specialists at the Moffett Center. The report does not support claims that thousands of inspectors were fired or that outbreaks resulted.
description_long: Reuters reported on April 17, 2025, that the Food and Drug Administration was suspending a proficiency-testing program for its Food Emergency Response Network after staffing cuts at the Department of Health and Human Services. The network’s program was intended to check the consistency and accuracy of about 170 laboratories that test food for pathogens and contaminants. Reuters reported that the cuts included a key quality-assurance officer, an analytical chemist, and two microbiologists at the Moffett Center. This is a specific laboratory quality-control interruption, not evidence that DOGE fired thousands of FDA food inspectors. The article does not establish that staffing changes caused later foodborne illness outbreaks or recalls. Those broader occupational and causal claims need evidence beyond the cited report. The corrected description keeps the supported event and affected program distinct from routine inspections, and it attributes the staffing explanation to the reporting rather than treating the story as proof of downstream consumer harm.
notes: Source-correction proposal only; no canonical or database record was changed.

title: HHS selects Tornillo for migrant-child shelter; facility opens in June 2018
description_short: HHS selected Tornillo on June 14, 2018; Texas Tribune reported the temporary shelter opened the next day with about 100 minors.
description_medium: HHS selected Tornillo Land Port of Entry near El Paso for a temporary shelter for children separated from parents; the Texas Tribune reported the site opened by June 15, 2018, with about 100 minors. Fort Bliss was among locations considered, but it was not the shelter described as opening. The cited reports do not substantiate claims about thousands housed, deaths, or blocked visits.
description_long: The Texas Tribune reported on June 14, 2018, that the Department of Health and Human Services had selected Tornillo Land Port of Entry near El Paso as a temporary shelter for migrant children separated from their parents under the administration’s zero-tolerance policy. A June 15 follow-up reported that the facility was operating and had about 100 minors on site at that time. The reporting distinguishes Tornillo from Fort Bliss: Fort Bliss and other military locations had been considered, but the temporary tent shelter described in these reports opened at Tornillo. This correction matters because the original title assigns the facility to the wrong location. The cited articles establish site selection, early opening, and a snapshot of initial occupancy. They do not establish that this site held thousands of children, that it had the specific conditions asserted in the original account, or that congressional visits were blocked. They also do not document deaths tied to this facility. Those claims would require facility-specific evidence and should not be imported from other locations or periods.

title: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to narrow birthright-citizenship injunctions
description_short: In March 2025, the administration asked the Supreme Court to narrow injunctions blocking Trump’s birthright-citizenship order.
description_medium: Reuters reported that the Justice Department asked the Supreme Court on March 13, 2025, to narrow injunctions blocking enforcement of Trump’s birthright-citizenship order. The request was a litigation application concerning the scope of court-ordered relief. It did not itself change courts’ authority or amount to an executive order stripping federal judges of power.
description_long: Reuters reported that the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court in March 2025 to limit the nationwide scope of injunctions blocking enforcement of President Donald Trump’s birthright-citizenship order. The Justice Department filed its requests on March 13, seeking narrower relief in the pending litigation. This was a legal argument about who could benefit from the injunctions and how broadly courts could pause the policy. It was not an executive order removing federal courts’ authority, and the filing did not itself change the law or determine the cases’ outcomes. The corrected entry should describe the procedural step and the requested remedy rather than the original claim that Trump issued a February measure stripping courts of power. The cited report supports the March litigation request; it does not support the original February date or a completed loss of judicial authority. Any later ruling or broader account of nationwide injunction doctrine is outside this specific filing event.

title: FY2026 budget proposed eliminating NEA amid grant disruptions
description_short: The FY2026 budget proposed eliminating the NEA; AP reported grant rejection and rescission notices and staff departures in May 2025.
description_medium: The Trump administration’s proposed FY2026 budget called for eliminating the National Endowment for the Arts. AP reported in May 2025 that dozens of organizations received grant rejection or rescission notices and that NEA staff were asked to resign or retire. These reports document a proposal and specific disruptions, not the abolition of NEA or NEH or the end of all federal arts funding.
description_long: The Trump administration’s proposed fiscal year 2026 budget called for eliminating the National Endowment for the Arts. The Associated Press reported on May 5, 2025, that dozens of organizations had received notices that grants were rejected or rescinded and that an NEA official said staff members had been asked to resign or retire. These reports describe a budget proposal and grantmaking disruptions. A proposed budget is not itself an enacted abolition, and the cited article does not establish that the National Endowment for the Arts or the National Endowment for the Humanities had been legally abolished in March 2025. It also does not establish that all federal arts and humanities support ended or document the original claims about simultaneous elimination of the Institute of Museum and Library Services and nationwide community impacts. The corrected account focuses on the NEA proposal and the specific notices and staffing actions AP reported. The number, value, and eventual disposition of all affected grants are not established by this article.
notes: Source-correction proposal only; no canonical or database record was changed.

title: ICE adds cell-site-simulator vehicles through an $825,000 contract modification
description_short: TechCrunch reported an $825,000 May 2025 ICE contract modification for additional vehicles equipped to support cell-site simulators.
description_medium: TechCrunch reported that ICE paid $825,000 for a May 8, 2025 contract modification buying additional cell-site-simulator vehicles, after a similar September 2024 contract. The reporting establishes procurement and the technology’s phone-location capability, not where or how often the vehicles were deployed, whom they targeted, warrant practices, or mass surveillance across immigrant neighborhoods.
description_long: TechCrunch reported on October 7, 2025, that Immigration and Customs Enforcement had paid $825,000 earlier that year for a contract modification covering additional cell-site-simulator vehicles. Public records described the May 8 award as a modification for additional vehicles supporting the Homeland Security Technical Operations program. The same vendor had signed a similar ICE contract in September 2024, before the Trump administration. Cell-site simulators imitate cell towers and can be used to detect or locate nearby phones, but a procurement record establishes equipment funding rather than operational practice. The article does not identify how often or where the additional vehicles were deployed, which people were targeted, what authorization applied to a particular use, or how information from nearby devices was handled. It therefore does not support the original claim of broad warrantless surveillance across immigrant neighborhoods or a proven Fourth Amendment violation. The corrected account records the documented purchase while leaving deployment and warrant questions unresolved.
